screens.title: Post-Launch Considerations & Portfolio Building
screens.narratorSegment: You’ve completed a major piece of work — your capstone — and that accomplishment opens a new phase. Post-launch is the period after you share a game where you gather player feedback, find lingering bugs, and decide whether to patch or iterate. Even for a student project, this process teaches you to prioritize fixes, read player reactions objectively, and make targeted updates. Equally important is turning the finished project into a portfolio entry that shows your skills. A strong portfolio entry includes a short, well-edited gameplay video, high-quality screenshots, a clear statement of your role and tools used, and ideally a playable demo so others can experience your work. In short, launch is not an endpoint but a transition: you shift from building features to listening, polishing, and communicating your work to others. Over the next screens, we’ll unpack how to collect and triage feedback, what to include in a portfolio entry, how to craft a gameplay video and playable demo, and practical next steps for continuous learning. Think about one thing in your project you are most proud of — that will be the core highlight of your portfolio entry.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Post-Launch & Portfolio
Post-Launch Considerations & Portfolio Building
How to iterate after launch and present your capstone so it opens doors.
In this lesson

You will learn how to collect player feedback, plan updates, and craft a portfolio entry with video, screenshots, and a playable demo.

Why it matters

Employers evaluate what you build. A clear, polished portfolio communicates skill, scope, and the ability to finish a project under constraints.

Explore Key Topics
Post-Launch
Gather feedback, triage bugs, and plan updates that respect your vision and resources.
Portfolio
Showcase your role, tech used, challenges solved, and provide a playable demo if possible.
Continuous Learning
Game jams, targeted study, and iteration are the path to steady improvement.
Capstone
Complete playable build that shows your skills.
Portfolio Entry
Video, screenshots, role, and demo.
Feedback Loop
Player feedback guides polish and future learning.
Connecting these pieces turns one project into ongoing learning and career evidence.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you’ll be able to treat your completed capstone as both a product in need of post-launch attention and as evidence of your abilities. First, you will understand basic post-launch activities: soliciting player feedback, identifying recurring bug reports, and planning minimal, high-impact updates. Second, you will recognize what makes a portfolio entry effective: a concise, compelling title and description, clear visuals, and a short gameplay video that demonstrates core mechanics. Third, you will learn how to assemble and present artifacts: a playable demo, a role statement that clarifies your contributions, a list of tools used, and a short reflection on challenges and learnings. Fourth, you will outline next steps for continuous growth, including participating in game jams and exploring targeted technical areas such as AI, networking, or optimization. Each objective supports practical skills recruiters look for: the ability to finish a project, polish it based on feedback, and communicate your role and decisions clearly. As you review the objective cards, think of one concrete example from your capstone that matches each objective so you can later use it in your portfolio or reflection.

screens.title: What is Post-Launch?
screens.narratorSegment: Post-launch is the phase after a game is first shared with players, focused on maintenance, responding to issues, and evolving the experience. For commercial projects this can mean months of updates; for a capstone it typically means a shorter cycle: gather feedback, reproduce and triage bugs, and plan a small set of fixes or polish items that fit your available time. A clear definition helps set expectations: post-launch is not about continuous feature expansion, but about targeted improvements that increase player satisfaction or clarity. A concrete example: you release a WebGL demo on a hosting platform and receive multiple reports that a jump input sometimes fails on mobile. Post-launch action would be to reproduce the issue, determine whether it’s an input mapping, physics timing, or UI overlay problem, and then implement a focused fix or fallback. A common misconception is thinking every piece of feedback must be implemented; instead, seek recurring patterns in reports and prioritize fixes that align with your design goals and time budget. The takeaway is to treat post-launch as a disciplined triage process: listen, reproduce, prioritize, and apply small, high-impact updates.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Post-launch is a short, disciplined cycle of feedback, reproduction, and targeted fixes rather than an open-ended list of feature requests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What is Post-Launch?
Definition & Scope
A focused cycle of listening, reproducing, and patching after release.
  • • Gather player feedback from platforms and friends.
  • • Reproduce reported issues and classify severity.
  • • Prioritize fixes that align with core gameplay and time budget.
  • • Plan small, testable updates or a patch and document changes.
Example
Multiple players report mobile jump inconsistency. Reproduce, check input mapping or UI blocking elements, apply fix, and release a small patch with a changelog note.
Key Takeaway

Treat post-launch as targeted maintenance: prioritize recurring issues that improve player understanding or core mechanics.

Common Mistake

Implementing every suggestion leads to scope creep. Instead, look for patterns and fix issues that improve the game's intent.

Triage Template
  1. 1) Issue summary
  2. 2) Steps to reproduce
  3. 3) Frequency / severity
  4. 4) Proposed fix and effort estimate
Pro tip
Keep changelogs brief: list fixes, version, and a short note on each change so players know what you shipped.

screens.title: Collecting and Acting on Feedback
screens.narratorSegment: Collecting feedback is simple in concept but requires method to be useful. Start with channels: friends, playtesters, platform comments, and issue trackers. When feedback arrives, reproduce the issue first; without reproduction you cannot estimate effort or cause. Next, classify each report by frequency and impact — a crash or blocker is high priority, a minor visual overlap is low. Group similar reports together; if ten players flag the same UI problem, it outranks a single feature request. Then estimate the effort needed and decide whether a patch, design tweak, or documentation change is the right response. A concrete example: ten players report difficulty understanding the jump timing. If reproduction shows unclear feedback on jump frames, consider a small animation or sound cue fix rather than a full rework. A common misconception is to equate vocal feedback with priority; instead, use patterns and severity. End each cycle with a short changelog entry and a note about whether you’d accept further suggestions. This process trains you to make pragmatic decisions and demonstrates to reviewers that you can manage an evolving product thoughtfully.

keyIdea.text: Reproduce, categorize, prioritize, estimate, and ship small fixes guided by repeated player signals.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Collecting Feedback
Feedback Channels & Reproduction
Use multiple input sources and always reproduce before planning fixes.
  • • Channels: friends, playtesters, itch.io comments, direct messages.
  • • Reproduce each report with clear steps and system details.
  • • Record device, build version, and exact steps to reproduce.
Example
Multiple reports about jump timing; reproduce, measure timing windows, then choose a fix: tweak windows or add feedback like sound.
Prioritization & Action
Classify by frequency and player impact to choose which fixes to ship first.
Prioritization Matrix
  • • High impact, high frequency: Immediate patch.
  • • High impact, low frequency: Investigate; schedule if reproducible.
  • • Low impact, high frequency: Consider usability tweaks.
  • • Low impact, low frequency: Document or defer.
Common Mistake

Number of comments does not always equal severity; look for recurring behavior that blocks play.

screens.title: Where to Share a Playable Demo
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing where to host a playable demo affects accessibility and how reviewers experience your work. A WebGL build hosted on a platform that supports browser play is often the most accessible: reviewers can play immediately without downloading. A downloadable PC executable can show more advanced tech or performance but requires extra friction: platform compatibility and trust. For a student capstone, itch. io is frequently the simplest choice because it supports both WebGL and downloadable builds and provides simple pages for video and screenshots. Another approach is to host a concise Web page (GitHub Pages or a personal site) that aggregates your video, screenshots, and demo links. A concrete example: publish a WebGL build for quick play and include a separate downloadable link for a higher-fidelity Windows build if needed. Common misconceptions include assuming every employer will run a large download; many prefer to see a quick playable experience first. Prioritize accessibility: make the demo easy to launch and include simple instructions, target hardware, and known issues so players know what to expect. Where to Share a Playable Demo means webgl offers immediate accessibility; downloadable builds allow fidelity but add friction — balance both if possible.. In practical terms, platforms and choices for hosting a webgl or downloadable build. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Where to Share
WebGL vs Downloadable
A quick comparison to choose the right delivery method for your demo.
WebGL: Immediate play in browser; best for showcasing mechanics quickly and getting low-friction feedback.
Downloadable: Higher fidelity and fewer engine limits, but requires downloads and may deter quick review.
Tip: provide both when possible — WebGL for casual reviewers, downloadable for deep inspection.
Platform Examples
  • • itch.io pages for WebGL and downloads with built-in media support.
  • • Personal portfolio site to centralize video, screenshots, and links.
  • • GitHub Pages for simple static aggregation of media and demo links.
Common Mistake

Assuming reviewers will run a large file; always offer a quick-play option and clear system notes.

screens.title: What to Include in a Portfolio Entry
screens.narratorSegment: A portfolio entry should tell a compact, convincing story about your project. At minimum include: a catchy title and one-paragraph description that hooks the viewer, several high-quality screenshots that show distinctive moments or UI, a short gameplay video that demonstrates core mechanics, and a playable demo if available. Also explicitly state your role and contributions so viewers know what you personally did. List the technologies used — Unity and C# plus any notable tools — and include a short reflection on challenges and learnings to show your problem-solving process. A concrete example: title the project with a memorable phrase, add a 2-3 sentence overview of genre and core mechanic, then show a 60–90 second video showcasing a level run and an enemy encounter. Misconception: don’t dump everything—avoid including raw asset lists or entire codebases without context. Instead, highlight key systems you implemented and provide links to in-depth docs like excerpts of a Game Design Document. The takeaway is to present a clear narrative: what the game is, what you did, how it was built, and what you learned. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Portfolio Contents
Essential Elements
  • • Catchy title and 1–2 sentence description.
  • • High-quality screenshots that show gameplay and UI.
  • • 1–3 minute gameplay video highlighting core mechanics.
  • • Playable demo (WebGL or downloadable) when possible.
Also include
Your role, technologies used (Unity, C#), and a short reflection on challenges and learnings.
Example Layout
  1. 1) Title & 2-line overview
  2. 2) 60–90s gameplay video
  3. 3) 4–5 screenshots
  4. 4) Role & Tools
  5. 5) Playable demo link and changelog excerpt
Key Takeaway

A concise, media-rich layout lets reviewers judge your work fast — make the most compelling evidence obvious.

screens.title: Writing a Concise Gameplay Video Script
screens.narratorSegment: A gameplay video is the single most effective portfolio asset. Plan it like a short storyboard: begin with a quick hook that shows the core mechanic in action within the first 10 seconds, then demonstrate a progression of moments that reveal controls, challenge, and feel. Keep clips short and use captions or brief overlays to highlight what the viewer should notice: core mechanic, unique twist, or a polished visual. Concrete example: start with the player's unique movement for four seconds, cut to an enemy encounter demonstrating combat for ten seconds, then show a short level traversal and an example of a player success state. Avoid long menus, loading screens, or slow pans. A common misconception is that longer footage proves depth; instead, a tight, edited 60–90 second video is easier to watch and shows confidence in what matters. End the video with a single frame that says where to play the demo and your role. This structure helps recruiters quickly grasp what sets your project apart and reduces friction to evaluate your skills. Writing a Concise Gameplay Video Script means hook, showcase core mechanic, highlight a challenge or level moment, and end with clear attribution and demo link.. In practical terms, what to show and why — a 60–90 second storyboard for your trailer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Gameplay Video
Storyboard Template (60–90s)
Plan each clip to communicate a single idea: mechanic, challenge, art, or polish.
00-08s: Hook — show core mechanic in action
08-25s: Mechanic in context — short level traversal
25-45s: Challenge or combat encounter
45-60s: Success or reward, polish moments
60-70s: Credits, role, and where to play
Editing Tips
  • • Keep cuts tight; avoid long idle shots.
  • • Use captions to highlight systems you built.
  • • Normalize audio and add subtle SFX to emphasize actions.
  • • End with a single clear callout: demo link and role.
Misconception

Long videos don’t impress. Recruiters want the core idea quickly; make the first 10 seconds irresistible.

screens.title: Documenting Your Role & Technologies
screens.narratorSegment: Clear role documentation is essential because reviewers need to know what parts of the project you delivered. Start by listing your formal role: Solo Developer, Lead Programmer, or Designer. Then provide 3–5 bullet contributions that are specific and measurable, for example: implemented player movement and combat systems, created tilemap levels, or developed the core gameplay loop in C#. Always attach technologies used explicitly — Unity, C#, and any notable tools like a pixel-art editor or audio middleware. A useful structure is: Role, Key Contributions, Tools, and a brief Challenges & Learnings paragraph. For instance, saying you implemented enemy AI with a patrol and chase state machine is stronger than saying you ‘worked on enemies.’ A common misconception is that code alone proves skill; instead, explain the design decisions behind your code and the impact on gameplay. Finally, include an optional Game Design Document excerpt or link to show planning skills. This documentation shows you can both build systems and communicate their purpose clearly. Documenting Your Role & Technologies means state your role and three specific contributions with tools used, and reflect briefly on challenges to show problem-solving.. In practical terms, how to explain what you did and the tools you used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Document Your Role
Role & Contributions Template
Role: Solo Developer
Key Contributions:
  • • Implemented player controller and physics interactions
  • • Built enemy AI with patrol and chase states
  • • Designed levels using Unity Tilemap system
Technologies & Reflection
Technologies: Unity, C#, Tilemap, Aseprite
Challenges & Learnings: Briefly state a problem and the solution, e.g., performance tuning via object pooling reduced GC spikes.

screens.title: Continuous Learning & Career Growth
screens.narratorSegment: Game development is a long-term craft. After your capstone, adopt a habit of focused practice. Start with short, time-boxed projects like game jams to reinforce prototyping skills and rapid decision-making. Pair that with a targeted technical goal — for example, one month of exploring AI behavior or three weeks learning object pooling and optimization. Keep a simple public record of these mini-projects: a short description, a build, and a short note on what you learned. Networking and community participation amplify learning: share progress on developer forums, ask for feedback, and join jams or local meetups. A common misconception is that large projects accelerate learning faster than many small, focused projects; in reality, deliberate short projects with reflection yield faster skill acquisition. The practical takeaway is a 90-day plan: one small jam, two week-long tech experiments, and an updated portfolio entry that includes the new work. screens.title: Handling Feedback — A Professional Approach
screens.narratorSegment: Responding to player feedback professionally is both a skill and part of your portfolio narrative. Start by reading feedback with curiosity rather than defensiveness. Record each piece of feedback in a log with tags such as UI, controls, difficulty, or crash. Look for recurring themes and quantify them when possible — five reports about an input issue is stronger evidence than one vague comment. Next, decide on an action: immediate fix, planned patch, or documented limitation. Always explain your decision in a changelog or reply — this shows you considered the report. For example, if multiple players flag frame drops on large enemy waves, you might prioritize object pooling or simplified effects. A misconception is to assume all feedback is equal; in practice, prioritize player-impacting issues that align with your design goals. Finally, view feedback as a growth tool: each clear changelog entry or considered response becomes part of your evidence that you can manage a product lifecycle responsibly. End with a short reflective note in your portfolio describing how you handled post-launch feedback. fullNarratorScript:
You’ve completed a major piece of work — your capstone — and that accomplishment opens a new phase. Post-launch is the period after you share a game where you gather player feedback, find lingering bugs, and decide whether to patch or iterate. Even for a student project, this process teaches you to prioritize fixes, read player reactions objectively, and make targeted updates. Equally important is turning the finished project into a portfolio entry that shows your skills. A strong portfolio entry includes a short, well-edited gameplay video, high-quality screenshots, a clear statement of your role and tools used, and ideally a playable demo so others can experience your work. In short, launch is not an endpoint but a transition: you shift from building features to listening, polishing, and communicating your work to others. Over the next screens, we’ll unpack how to collect and triage feedback, what to include in a portfolio entry, how to craft a gameplay video and playable demo, and practical next steps for continuous learning. Think about one thing in your project you are most proud of — that will be the core highlight of your portfolio entry.

By the end of these screens you’ll be able to treat your completed capstone as both a product in need of post-launch attention and as evidence of your abilities. First, you will understand basic post-launch activities: soliciting player feedback, identifying recurring bug reports, and planning minimal, high-impact updates. Second, you will recognize what makes a portfolio entry effective: a concise, compelling title and description, clear visuals, and a short gameplay video that demonstrates core mechanics. Third, you will learn how to assemble and present artifacts: a playable demo, a role statement that clarifies your contributions, a list of tools used, and a short reflection on challenges and learnings. Fourth, you will outline next steps for continuous growth, including participating in game jams and exploring targeted technical areas such as AI, networking, or optimization. Each objective supports practical skills recruiters look for: the ability to finish a project, polish it based on feedback, and communicate your role and decisions clearly. As you review the objective cards, think of one concrete example from your capstone that matches each objective so you can later use it in your portfolio or reflection.

This second objectives screen shows how to turn each learning goal into concrete portfolio evidence. For post-launch work, a triage log or short changelog entry proves you can process feedback and prioritize fixes. For portfolio construction, include a one- to two-paragraph description and a 1–3 minute gameplay video that highlights core mechanics; this shows you can communicate design and technical intent. For role documentation, list three to five specific contributions such as systems you coded, art you produced, or design you led — naming exact systems gives credibility. For continuous learning, show a short plan: what you’ll practice next and one small project or game jam you’ll complete in the next quarter. Each of these items is an artifact a recruiter can inspect quickly. When you prepare your portfolio entry, imagine someone has 30 seconds to judge your work; prioritize a clear highlight, an evidence video, and a direct statement of your role. This screen prepares you to convert goals into verifiable artifacts.

Post-launch is the phase after a game is first shared with players, focused on maintenance, responding to issues, and evolving the experience. For commercial projects this can mean months of updates; for a capstone it typically means a shorter cycle: gather feedback, reproduce and triage bugs, and plan a small set of fixes or polish items that fit your available time. A clear definition helps set expectations: post-launch is not about continuous feature expansion, but about targeted improvements that increase player satisfaction or clarity. A concrete example: you release a WebGL demo on a hosting platform and receive multiple reports that a jump input sometimes fails on mobile. Post-launch action would be to reproduce the issue, determine whether it’s an input mapping, physics timing, or UI overlay problem, and then implement a focused fix or fallback. A common misconception is thinking every piece of feedback must be implemented; instead, seek recurring patterns in reports and prioritize fixes that align with your design goals and time budget. The takeaway is to treat post-launch as a disciplined triage process: listen, reproduce, prioritize, and apply small, high-impact updates.

Collecting feedback is simple in concept but requires method to be useful. Start with channels: friends, playtesters, platform comments, and issue trackers. When feedback arrives, reproduce the issue first; without reproduction you cannot estimate effort or cause. Next, classify each report by frequency and impact — a crash or blocker is high priority, a minor visual overlap is low. Group similar reports together; if ten players flag the same UI problem, it outranks a single feature request. Then estimate the effort needed and decide whether a patch, design tweak, or documentation change is the right response. A concrete example: ten players report difficulty understanding the jump timing. If reproduction shows unclear feedback on jump frames, consider a small animation or sound cue fix rather than a full rework. A common misconception is to equate vocal feedback with priority; instead, use patterns and severity. End each cycle with a short changelog entry and a note about whether you’d accept further suggestions. This process trains you to make pragmatic decisions and demonstrates to reviewers that you can manage an evolving product thoughtfully.

Choosing where to host a playable demo affects accessibility and how reviewers experience your work. A WebGL build hosted on a platform that supports browser play is often the most accessible: reviewers can play immediately without downloading. A downloadable PC executable can show more advanced tech or performance but requires extra friction: platform compatibility and trust. For a student capstone, itch. io is frequently the simplest choice because it supports both WebGL and downloadable builds and provides simple pages for video and screenshots. Another approach is to host a concise Web page (GitHub Pages or a personal site) that aggregates your video, screenshots, and demo links. A concrete example: publish a WebGL build for quick play and include a separate downloadable link for a higher-fidelity Windows build if needed. Prioritize accessibility: make the demo easy to launch and include simple instructions, target hardware, and known issues so players know what to expect. Responding to player feedback professionally is both a skill and part of your portfolio narrative. Start by reading feedback with curiosity rather than defensiveness. Record each piece of feedback in a log with tags such as UI, controls, difficulty, or crash. Look for recurring themes and quantify them when possible — five reports about an input issue is stronger evidence than one vague comment. Next, decide on an action: immediate fix, planned patch, or documented limitation. Always explain your decision in a changelog or reply — this shows you considered the report. For example, if multiple players flag frame drops on large enemy waves, you might prioritize object pooling or simplified effects. A misconception is to assume all feedback is equal; in practice, prioritize player-impacting issues that align with your design goals. Finally, view feedback as a growth tool: each clear changelog entry or considered response becomes part of your evidence that you can manage a product lifecycle responsibly. End with a short reflective note in your portfolio describing how you handled post-launch feedback. Here are six compact concepts to remember from this chapter, starting with three on this screen. First, Post-Launch: the maintenance and update phase after an initial release where you triage bugs and listen to players. Second, Portfolio: a curated set of artifacts — video, screenshots, playable demo, role statement — that demonstrate your skills. Third, Gameplay Video: a short edited clip that shows your core mechanic and feel; it’s often the most persuasive single asset in a portfolio. Each concept is a shorthand you can use when planning what to publish and how to describe your project. Keeping these ideas short helps you prioritize what to show first when someone visits your portfolio. Later we’ll summarize the remaining concepts — playable demo, game jam, and continuous learning — and provide a compact takeaway you can act on immediately.

These last three concepts complete the short glossary you’ll use when preparing and presenting your work. Playable Demo: a link or build that lets others experience the game firsthand; it’s the strongest proof but requires careful packaging and instructions. Game Jam: a time-boxed event to practice rapid prototyping and add new, focused projects to your portfolio. Continuous Learning: an ongoing habit of experimenting, updating your portfolio, and reflecting on what you learned. Together these concepts guide your post-capstone plan: provide a low-friction demo, keep learning through short projects, and publish concise artifacts that show growth. The final, actionable takeaway is to pick one highlight from your capstone, create a 60–90 second video of it, and publish a minimal playable demo or WebGL build with a short role statement — that single step dramatically improves how others perceive your work.
